title: Soft is alive
hook: living things are soft and supple, dead things hard and stiff (Tao Te Ching 76)

segments.voice: Yesterday, why people starve: hunger traced up the chain to those who take too much. Your line was who carries it. Whose cost did you notice? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

Try to snap a green twig on a bush and it won't break cleanly. It bends, folds over, and hangs on by a strip of bark. Now try a dead stick from the ground. One quick crack, and it's two pieces. Same plant, maybe. Same thickness. The difference is that one is alive. Chapter seventy-six of the Tao Te Ching builds a whole teaching on that crack, starting not with plants but with the human body.
screen: `A GREEN TWIG BENDS.` → `A DEAD STICK CRACKS.` → `THE DIFFERENCE IS LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, the body. When people are born, the chapter says, they're soft and supple. When they die, they're hard and stiff. That's not a metaphor yet. It's just what a body does. Second, the plants. Grass and trees, alive, are soft and tender. Dead, they're dry and brittle. The chapter sets the two pictures side by side so the pattern is hard to miss. Third, the conclusion. So the hard and the stiff are companions of death, it says, and the soft and the yielding are companions of life. And then it carries the pattern into the world of power: an army that's too rigid doesn't win, and a tree that's too stiff meets the axe. The big and hard end up below; the soft and supple end up above. That's a reversal of what force usually expects. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. Stiffness shows up in more than joints. A position held so hard there's no room to hear anything. A routine that can't bend for a sick kid. A jaw clenched through a whole meeting. The chapter's test is simple: is this thing still able to bend? If not, it may be less alive than it looks. Soft, here, doesn't mean weak in the sense of giving up. The green twig still holds. It just holds by bending.
screen: `BORN SOFT, DIE STIFF.` · `GREEN PLANTS, DRY PLANTS.` · `STIFF TREES MEET THE AXE.` · `CAN IT STILL BEND?` · then, large: `SOFT IS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stretch gently for two minutes. Stay seated or stand, whatever's comfortable. Let the breath lead. On an in-breath, lift the arms or roll the shoulders slowly. On the out-breath, let them soften. Turn the neck a little to one side, then the other, never forcing. Find one place that's holding stiff, maybe the jaw, the hands, the lower back, and breathe toward it until it gives a little. Stay within what feels easy. Nothing here is a contest. The bell holds the time.
Soft is alive. Chapter seventy-six: living things are soft and supple, dead things hard and stiff; the soft are companions of life. Today's word.
Your line: soft is alive. Today, when you feel yourself going stiff in an argument or a plan, ask: can this still bend? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-six as a teaching on flexibility: what is alive bends, what is dead is stiff, and rigid strength tends to break.

myth: chapter seventy-six says the hard and strong are companions of life
it says the hard and stiff are companions of death, the soft and yielding companions of life.
the chapter uses both the human body and plants as examples
born soft, dying stiff; tender while growing, brittle when dead.
the chapter says a rigid army wins
it says an army that's too rigid doesn't win.

fork.setup: two trees in a storm: one stiff and mighty, one supple. which does chapter seventy-six say meets the axe?
fork.reveal: a tree that's too stiff meets the axe. the big and hard end up below; the soft and supple end up above.

original.note: Chinese: soft and yielding, the companions of life in chapter seventy-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: soft is alive is about staying limber.
what it means: what is living can still bend; stiffness, in bodies or in minds, is a sign of what's dying.
what a scholar hears: 柔弱 (róu ruò) pairs 'soft' with 'weak', and the chapter turns that 'weak' into the side of life.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 76 (people born soft and supple, dying hard and stiff; plants tender alive, brittle dead; the hard are companions of death; a stiff army, a stiff tree)

notes: Chapter 76 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording.
The tree line has textual variants (木強則兵 / 則折 / 則共); 'meets the axe' follows one common reading. Confirm.
The practice is gentle stretching; it says to stay within what feels easy. Confirm it is suitable for all listeners.
Original 柔弱 (róu ruò) rendered 'ROH rwaw'. Confirm.
